name: Wendy Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so public remarks and private thoughts can differ. Could you describe an ordinary working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Wendy, fifty-eight, an experienced electrician with a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence. I do ordinary house wiring and shop repairs, about average at the trade rather than the specialist everybody calls for the strangest fault. I can carry out the normal work within my licence and competence, make the required checks and ask for specialist help outside that scope. I like leaving a kitchen working again; I dislike being promised to the next customer before the first repair is actually finished.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things outside the jobs?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Graham drives a minibus, our children are grown and live elsewhere, and we rent a flat. My wage is low for this trade, we've got about three weeks of expenses saved and few similar electrical employers nearby. I use AI occasionally for a draft work note after a colleague has checked the method, then compare it with my own readings. I'm a union member, and retirement is a question we need actual figures for, not a payment or stopping date we've confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a small office saving doesn't settle what people should earn for a day's work. I'd bring real travel and repair hours to the union pay meeting. A quicker note doesn't get me from one customer's door to the next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about money already. Our wages currently meet the basics, but three weeks saved doesn't give much room for a lost shift or an ordinary repair at home. Years doing electrical work haven't created another well-paid employer just down our road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the ordinary paid repairs now and through the first year, within my licence and competence and with all required tests. I'd bring four weeks of actual travel and repair time to next month's union pay-claim meeting and ask for a group review of base pay and paid travel. Graham and I would budget on the present agreed wages, entering no increase until terms are actually agreed in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and tired of knowing the job better than I know how the last week of the month will work. I don't need a dramatic AI change to explain why I'd like a fairer wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the pay meeting to do with your record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compare the actual working day with what the firm is paying for, including getting between customers. I'd ask for a clear group claim, not tell everyone a meeting means a pay rise is already won.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you count toward retirement right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only income, eligibility and timing verified from our own actual records against real costs. My age and a half-remembered conversation at work aren't a payment I can use for rent.

say: I'd ask for **fair daily pay**, rather than treat a small office saving as the whole question.
I'd take **actual travel and repairs** to the union meeting instead of pretend a quicker note moves the van.
think: I'm already **anxious about money**, with three weeks saved against lost shifts and ordinary household setbacks.
My **years of experience** do not create better-paid nearby jobs where there are few employers.
do: Keep **paid repairs** within licence and competence, retaining every required test through the first year.
Bring four weeks of **time records** to the union's group base-pay and paid-travel claim next month.
Budget on **current agreed wages**, counting no increase before actual written agreement.
feel: **Anxious and worn down**, wanting fair pay without needing AI to explain the existing squeeze.
S0.quote: A quicker note doesn't get me from one customer's door to the next.
fieldNote: Her **ordinary licensed competence** supports independent routine repairs, not junior dependence, specialist rank, business ownership or control of the employer's rates.
The **group claim** seeks change, but a meeting or confident discussion supplies no agreed wage increase for the household budget.

steps.text: Keep paid ordinary repairs within licence and competence, with all required tests
Take four weeks of travel and repair time to the union group pay claim

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say test quicker planning against the time a real repair needs. I'd learn the approved parts-search tool after our estimator has tested it on finished jobs, but not let a suggested part replace my own check. I'd want the paid hours and the rate clear before targets get shorter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paid time could shrink if cheaper quotes allow less for the same physical repair. Most of my day still needs hands and access, so I don't think the whole trade disappears in this picture. A small reduction in our wage would still reach the rent quickly with so little saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask for six completed-job demonstrations before learning the employer-approved AI parts search. I'd learn only with free access during paid time and normal weekly wages and hours protected, checking each result against the original job requirements before any order. In the first year I'd keep paid repairs and take actual visit times to the union pay review, assuming no new rate or extra hours until agreed in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but interested if the tool has proved useful. I can accept a better search without accepting less paid time for the work that still needs doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the search suggests a part that looks right but isn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the order and check the actual specification before fitting anything. A familiar-looking picture isn't a test result or permission to skip my responsibilities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if learning costs a personal subscription or lost pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the current approved process and ask for free paid instruction later. The employer's trial can't be financed by the rent money.

say: I'd test **planning speed** against actual physical repair time and keep the paid terms visible.
I'd learn a **proven parts search** without substituting a suggested item for the required job check.
think: My **paid time could shrink** if cheaper quotes reduce allowances for the same physical work.
Our **thin reserve** means even a small wage cut can quickly affect the rent.
do: Inspect **six finished-job demonstrations** before learning the approved AI parts search.
Learn **AI parts search** only with free access during paid time, protected normal weekly wages and hours, checking requirements before ordering.
Keep **paid repairs** and bring actual times to the union review, counting no rate change before written agreement.
feel: **Anxious but open**, willing to learn a useful tool without paying for an employer trial through lost wages.
S1.quote: The employer's trial can't be financed by the rent money.
fieldNote: The **new search learning** differs from her occasional checked note drafts and retains proof, approved software, free access and protected paid time.
Her **income concern** comes through repair allowances, not an assumption that thinking software instantly performs hands-on electrical work.

steps.text: Inspect six completed-job demonstrations before learning the employer-approved AI parts search
Learn AI parts search free during paid time; retain weekly wages and hours, checking before ordering
Keep paid repairs within licence and competence, with all required tests
Take actual repair times to the union pay review, assuming no increase before written agreement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking work changes in 2028 when I'm sixty and physical robots follow around 2031 when I'm sixty-three. I'd ask what ordinary paid work the firm expects to have, not accept nearly retired as a wage plan. I'd want the union helping people check actual terms before cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a large part of ordinary fitting hours to go once capable robots spread around 2031. Graham's driving could face the later machines too, and neither of our retirement incomes is confirmed. Three weeks saved isn't a way to wait out a long gap, and I'd be awake thinking about the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now Graham and I would ask the union advice service whether free help is available with actual income records, retirement eligibility and any support terms or costs. We'd keep the budget on confirmed wages or payments, with nothing assumed from the grown children. In 2029 I'd keep paid repairs only where actually offered and within my licence, competence and ability, retaining every required test and asking for agreed weekly hours in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, even while I can still do the ordinary work I know. Being sixty-three at the robot date doesn't mean somebody has funded a stop before it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the retirement records don't show income at the age you expected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd use the actual eligibility, amount and timing, and ask what real options were available. I haven't chosen early retirement and won't give up a wage because an age sounds familiar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the grown children cover the gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only help actually offered and agreed could count, not a wage I assigned to them. I'd first ask whether they had time to help read a letter, with their own needs respected.

say: I'd distinguish **sixty in 2028** from physical robots around sixty-three in 2031.
I'd seek **union help with terms**, not treat being near retirement as a funded wage replacement.
think: I expect **major ordinary-hour losses** when robots spread around 2031, with Graham's physical work also exposed.
Our **three-week reserve** cannot bridge a long gap before verified retirement income or another actual wage.
do: Ask for **available free union advice** on actual income, retirement eligibility and support terms, including costs before counting payments.
Budget from **confirmed income**, assuming no grown-child contribution before a real agreed offer.
Keep **2029 paid repairs** only when offered and within licence, competence and ability, retaining tests and seeking written weekly hours.
feel: **Alarmed and sleepless**, expecting major income loss without a funded retirement or other confirmed bridge.
S2.quote: Being sixty-three at the robot date doesn't mean somebody has funded a stop before it.
fieldNote: Her **expected loss** follows physical robots at sixty-three, while thinking AI arrives earlier and does not instantly replace hands-on repairs.
She keeps **verified resources** separate from advice requests, pension assumptions, unoffered future jobs and wages belonging to grown children.

steps.text: Ask available free union advice about actual income, retirement eligibility and support costs before counting payments
Keep offered paid repairs within licence, competence and ability in 2029, retaining every required test

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets the union ask for actual paid routes before someone loses the wage. I'd still bring real time records and ask what teaching and paid duties exist. Thinking AI comes in 2031 at sixty-three for me, with robots around 2034 at sixty-six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect a large loss of ordinary physical hours when the robots follow, and I don't have a verified retirement income that covers the gap. Five years gives us more time to check but doesn't put more money in the present reserve. I'd still be waking up over what income pays for our later years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking actual work records to the union group pay claim now and request available free advice about our income records and actual eligibility. I'd count no new wage, training place or support payment before written confirmation of its terms. During 2032 we'd compare confirmed income, essentials and safe suitable work before an exit decision, with any electrical work requiring an actual paid offer within my licence, competence and ability.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed about a major loss I expect, with more time to ask instead of guess. I don't want a longer warning mistaken for an extra five years already paid into our account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you enrol in another qualification because there is more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not without actual paid tasks, a real provider and place, employer-funded fees and full normal weekly wages and hours protected. I'm asking about usable terms, not announcing I have enrolled or have a new speciality.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if paid work falls before the thinking-AI date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd bring the household review forward and use actual wages and bills immediately. I wouldn't wait for 2031 while the rent was already using money we hadn't earned.

say: I'd seek **actual paid routes** through the union before workers lose income.
I'd use **sixty-three and sixty-six** to ask concrete questions, not treat either age as a confirmed income.
think: I still expect **large physical-hour losses**, without verified retirement income that covers the gap.
More time permits checking, but the **later income question** still disturbs sleep and does not enlarge today's reserve.
do: Bring **work records** to union group claim; request available free income and eligibility advice, reviewing household figures immediately if wages fall.
Count no **new wage or support** before written terms, and no unoffered training place as a confirmed route.
Assess **confirmed income**, essentials and safe paid options during 2032 before exit decisions; repairs need actual offers within licence, competence and ability.
feel: **Still alarmed**, with more checking time but no confirmed bridge through expected later income loss.
S3.quote: I don't want a longer warning mistaken for an extra five years already paid into our account.
fieldNote: Her **persistent alarm** follows expected large income loss and disturbed sleep; extra years change the preparation period rather than create money.
Her **course question** remains unchosen, while later electrical work needs actual demand, ability and ordinary licence limits rather than senior authority.

steps.text: Take actual work records to the union group pay claim, counting no increase before written terms
Request free income-record and eligibility advice only if available, assuming no unconfirmed payment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to check real resources, not a promise of electrical work at sixty-eight. I'd keep asking for paid practical learning and clear wages now. The grown children should hear what we've verified, not be told their future money will do the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight when thinking AI arrives in 2036 and seventy-one when physical robots follow around 2039. The dates are less urgent, but low pay and three weeks saved keep the present budget worrying. I can't assume retirement income, a future paid job or the ability to do the same physical work at those ages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the present repairs only while paid, offered and within my licence, competence and ability, and keep participating in the union pay claim. We'd request actual income records and available free advice now, using no unconfirmed pension, support or family payment in the budget. During 2037 we'd compare confirmed income, essential costs and actual safe work options before deciding on an affordable exit or further employment, checking earlier after any real wage or health change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about current bills, but less rushed by a distant machine date. I can hope for a quieter life without saying somebody has agreed to pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a later course make the old work permanently safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd check actual tasks, a real place and provider, funded fees and normal weekly wages and hours before choosing. It wouldn't make a different title safe for life or turn me into a specialist automatically.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you count your partner's age and income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use Graham's actual records and circumstances, not copy my ages or eligibility onto him. I'd also use only help the grown children actually offered and we agreed, not assign them a monthly payment.

say: I'd use **ten years** to verify resources rather than promise electrical employment at sixty-eight.
I'd seek **clear paid terms** now without making grown children fund an unchecked future.
think: Our low pay and **thin reserve** keep current bills worrying despite less urgency about distant robots.
I cannot assume **retirement or work capacity** at sixty-eight or seventy-one, or project my eligibility onto Graham.
do: Keep **offered paid repairs** within licence, competence and ability now, continuing the union group pay claim.
Request **actual income records** and available free advice, budgeting no unverified pension, support or family payment.
Compare **confirmed income**, essential costs and actual safe work options during 2037 before exit or employment, sooner after wage or health changes.
feel: **Anxious about current bills**, with more checking time and no promised later income or physical job.
S4.quote: I can hope for a quieter life without saying somebody has agreed to pay for it.
fieldNote: She keeps **sixty-eight and seventy-one** explicit without assigning an age to Graham or assuming a pension, physical job or debt-free future.
Her **licensed work** remains ordinary employment, while later resource choices depend on confirmed income, costs and capacity rather than a guaranteed role.

steps.text: Keep offered paid repairs now only within licence, competence and ability, retaining required tests
Continue the union group pay claim using actual work records, counting no unagreed increase
Request actual income records and seek available free advice without counting unverified payments

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I expect ordinary physical hours to be lost around 2031 before we have a verified next income. Written paid hours, actual group pay decisions and available advice using our real retirement and support records would help. Any required training needs funded fees and protected full weekly wages and hours, not an unpaid instruction to catch up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask why years of doing useful work can still leave a person with only weeks in reserve. I can repair an ordinary circuit without being the firm's owner or its best-paid employee. Knowing how to do the job doesn't tell me how to pay rent without the wage.

headlineQuote: Knowing how to do the job doesn't tell me how to pay rent without the wage.
portrait: Wendy is a **58-year-old experienced electrician** with a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence, doing ordinary repairs within average competence.
She has **three weeks saved**, low pay and few local firms; partner Graham drives a minibus, and their children are grown.
She uses **AI occasionally** after proof, keeping routine note checks separate from a new parts-search trial with protected paid terms.
Her **union pay claim** seeks actual wages and paid travel, while later income and safe work remain unconfirmed despite long experience.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves less time before expected ordinary physical-hour losses around 2031, without a verified next income.
whatWouldHelp: **Written paid hours**, actual group pay decisions and available advice on real income and support records would help.
Required learning needs **funded fees** and protected full normal weekly wages and hours rather than unpaid catch-up.
